newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Norminco blames title ruling for woes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Norminco blames title ruling for woes.

text.p: Australian tin miner Norminco Ltd said on Thursday it believed a court ruling on Aboriginal land claims -- known as the Wik decision -- was to blame for the difficulties which resulted in it going into receivership.
"We're the first victims of the Wik decision," Gary Allen, chief executive officer of Norminco, told Reuters.

Allen said advanced negotiations over A$1.1 million in funding for the mine with the Suncorp-Metway-Queensland Industrial Development Corp (QIDC) group were abruptly cancelled on Friday, leading to its chief lender Macquarie Bank to refuse
to extend loan facilities amounting to around A$500,000.

The QIDC group abandoned the talks after the state government suspended the issue and renewal of mining leases because of the federal court's Wik ruling in December that pastoral leases due not automatically extinguish claims of ownership to land by indigineous peoples, Allen said.
Queensland previously held the view that pastoral leases overrode native title claims.

Trading in Norminco shares was suspended earlier on Thursday and mining of the Leichhardt Creek alluvial tin deposits in north Queensland has stopped, Allen said. The company has been placed under the management of receivers Ferrier Hodgson.

An official of Macquarie Bank declined to and Martin Links of Ferrier Hodgson said he was not yet fully aware of all the circumstances leading to the receivership. "All I know is that there is a default in the finance agreement," Links said.
A spokesman for QIDC would say only that it was "very early days" regarding the implications of Queensland's interpretation of the Wik ruling on the mining industry as a whole.
After weathering operational and financial difficulties since the the remote mine's commissioning in 1995, Norminco was starting to show profits, Allen said.
Production was at a rate of one tonne of high-grade tin concentrate a day, which was being sold to a Malaysian smelter.
Part of Norminco's early financial difficulties arose from a tight liquidity situation due to below-budget tin production.
Queensland Premier Bob Borbidge said on Thursday that up to 85 percent of the state could be subject to land title claims from Aboriginal groups as a result of the Wik ruling.
The decision was named after the Wik Aboriginal group, which won on appeal the right to contest ownership of 35,000 square kilometres of land in Queensland.

In 1992, the high court overturned the historical idea of terra nullus -- that Australia was an empty land when white settlers arrived in 1788 -- thus recognising that Aborigines had traditional land rights.
In 1993, the former Labor Australian government passed legislation allowing Aborigines to claim land if they could prove uninterrupted traditional usage of that land.
Talks between Norminco and a substitute lender were well advanced and it was hoped the mine would resume operating at some point, Allen said.
